cues.text: At around two in the morning on April 17, 1560, during the octave of Easter, a Franciscan friar named Brother Angelo Blasi woke at Morrovalle, Italy.
He heard violent crackling and looked out to see the church engulfed in flames.
He roused the rest of the community, but it took seven hours to bring the blaze fully under control, by which time the church itself lay largely in ruins.
In the days that followed, the friars began the slow work of clearing the wreckage of the main altar.
On April 27, ten days after the fire, Father Battista da Ascoli was removing marble from the ruined altar.
He uncovered a pyx wedged in a cavity in the wall, its outer case scorched black by the fire except for the lid, and its linen corporal singed at the edges.
Inside, the consecrated Host was found completely intact and in good condition, having survived seven hours of fire that had consumed the church around it.
Father Battista's cry at the discovery drew a crowd, and for three full days afterward the recovered Host was exposed for public adoration before the community.
Pope Pius IV, informed of the event, dispatched Ludovico di Forli, Bishop of Bertinoro, to Morrovalle to investigate its authenticity in person.

On receiving the bishop's report, Pius IV judged the preservation to be without natural explanation and issued a bull authorizing public devotion to the relic, which was placed afterward in an ivory case for veneration.

Morrovalle marked the fourth centenary of the event in 1960, and the town council voted to inscribe its main gate with the words Civitas Eucaristica — Eucharistic City — a title the town has carried ever since.

The relic remains in the church of San Bartolomeo, a fire-scarred survivor whose story rests less on transformation than on the plain, specific fact of what a marble cavity happened to shield from seven hours of flame.
